sentences.nl: Hallo.
sentences.en: Hello.

sentences.nl: Ik ben Bart de Pau,, online docent Nederlands.
sentences.en: I am Bart de Pau, online Dutch teacher.

sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar, les 14 (over verkleinwoorden), en les 15 (over rangtelwoorden).
sentences.en: Today we practice Dutch sentences with the grammar from #dutchgrammar, lesson 14 (about diminutives), and lesson 15 (about ordinal numbers).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we Dutch sentences, with the grammar of #dutchgrammar, lesson 14 (about diminutives), and lesson 15 (about ordinal numbers).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Vandaag oefenen we" follows the standard Dutch word order for main clauses: [Time] + [Verb] + [Subject].  
• "met de grammatica van" uses "met" (with) to indicate accompaniment and "van" (of) to specify possession or relation.  
• "verkleinwoorden" (diminutives) and "rangtelwoorden" (ordinal numbers) are compound nouns, commonly formed in Dutch.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Morgen leren we nieuwe woorden." (Tomorrow we learn new words.)  
  - "Ik praat met de leraar van de school." (I talk with the teacher of the school.)  
  - "Ik hou van Nederlandse lessen." (I love Dutch lessons.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Vandaag bespreken we de regels van de Nederlandse taal." (Today we discuss the rules of the Dutch language.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• In the Dutch educational context, "les" (lesson) often refers to a specific topic or chapter in a textbook or course, which is typically how structured language courses are organized.

sentences.nl: Dit zijn Martin en Marieke.
sentences.en: These are Martin and Marieke.

sentences.nl: Martin gaat vanavond voor Marieke koken.
sentences.en: Martin is going to cook for Marieke tonight.

sentences.nl: Ze komen van de markt.
sentences.en: They are coming from the market.

sentences.nl: Martin woont in een appartement op de vijfde verdieping.
sentences.en: Martin lives in an apartment on the fifth floor.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin lives in an apartment on the fifth floor.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Woont" is the third person singular form of "wonen," meaning "to live."  
• "In een appartement" uses the preposition "in," meaning "in" or "inside."  
• "Op de vijfde verdieping" uses "op" to indicate location, meaning "on the fifth floor."  
• Word order follows the typical Subject-Verb-Object pattern in Dutch.

• Examples:  
  - "Zij werkt in een kantoor op de tweede verdieping." (She works in an office on the second floor.)  
  - "De kat slaapt op de bank in de woonkamer." (The cat sleeps on the couch in the living room.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Lisa studeert in de bibliotheek op de derde verdieping." (Lisa studies in the library on the third floor.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, floors are usually counted starting from the ground floor as "begane grond," followed by the first floor being "eerste verdieping." This is different from the US system, where the first floor is typically at ground level.

sentences.nl: Voor Marieke is dit de eerste keer bij Martin thuis.
sentences.en: For Marieke, this is the first time at Martin's home.

sentences.nl: ‘Wat een gezellig appartementje!’, zegt Marieke.
sentences.en: "What a cozy little apartment!" says Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• "What a cozy little apartment!" says Marieke.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat een" is an exclamatory phrase often used to express surprise or admiration.  
• "Gezellig" is a Dutch word with no direct English equivalent, capturing warmth, coziness, and friendliness.  
• The suffix "-je" in "appartementje" is a diminutive, indicating smallness or affection.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Wat een mooie dag!" (What a beautiful day!)  
  - "Wat een leuk hondje!" (What a cute little dog!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wat een prachtig schilderijtje!" (What a beautiful little painting!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The word "gezellig" is deeply embedded in Dutch culture and is often used to describe social gatherings, environments, or even people that create a pleasant and warm atmosphere.

sentences.nl: Ja, ik woon hier heel graag.
sentences.en: Yes, I really enjoy living here.

sentences.nl: Straks laat ik het huis zien.
sentences.en: Later, I will show the house.

sentences.nl: Maar we hebben honger!
sentences.en: But we are hungry!

sentences.nl: Dus eerst gaan we koken.
sentences.en: So first we are going to cook.

sentences.nl: Ze lopen naar het keukentje.
sentences.en: They walk to the kitchenette.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• They walk to the small kitchen.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ze" is a pronoun meaning "they."  
• "Lopen" is the verb "to walk" in the present tense.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to."  
• "Het keukentje" is a diminutive form of "keuken" (kitchen), meaning "the small kitchen." The suffix "-tje" is commonly used to create diminutives in Dutch.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Hij loopt naar de winkel." (He walks to the store.)  
  - "Ze speelt met het hondje." (She plays with the little dog.)  
  - "We gaan naar het park." (We go to the park.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ze rennen naar het tuintje. (They run to the little garden.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives like "-tje" is frequent in Dutch and can convey endearment or smallness. Dutch speakers often use diminutives to soften statements or to refer lovingly to objects and people.

sentences.nl: Kun je helpen met koken? — Natuurlijk.
sentences.en: Can you help with cooking? — Of course.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kun je helpen met koken? — Natuurlijk.  
  (Can you help with cooking? — Naturally.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Kun je" is a question structure using "kunnen" (can) in an informal tone. It places the modal verb "kun" before the subject "je".  
• "Helpen met" means "help with," where "met" is the preposition used to indicate the activity.  
• "Natuurlijk" is an adverb meaning "naturally" or "of course," used to affirm a statement.

• Examples:  
  - Kun je me bellen? (Can you call me?)  
  - Helpen met de voorbereidingen is belangrijk. (Helping with the preparations is important.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kun je de deur openen? — Natuurlijk. (Can you open the door? — Naturally.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it's common to use "natuurlijk" in a friendly and informal setting to agree to a request or suggestion, showing willingness and openness.

sentences.nl: Wil je ondertussen iets drinken? — Nou, ik lust wel een biertje.
sentences.en: Would you like something to drink in the meantime? — Well, I could go for a beer.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Will you in-the-meantime something drink? — Well, I crave indeed a beer.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wil je" is an informal way to ask someone if they want something, using "willen" (to want).  
• "Ondertussen" means "in the meantime" and is used to suggest doing something while waiting or during another activity.  
• "Lust" comes from "lusten," meaning "to like" or "to crave," often used with food and drinks.

  • "Wil je wat eten?" (Do you want something to eat?)  
  • "Hij lust geen koffie." (He doesn't like coffee.)  
  • "Ondertussen werkte hij aan zijn project." (In the meantime, he worked on his project.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wil je ondertussen even zitten?" (Do you want to sit down in the meantime?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it is common to offer guests something to drink when they arrive at your home as a sign of hospitality.

sentences.nl: Pak zelf maar.
sentences.en: Help yourself.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• "Take yourself just."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Pak" is the imperative form of the verb "pakken," meaning "to take" or "to grab."  
• "Zelf" means "yourself," emphasizing that the person should do it independently.  
• "Maar" is often used to make a command or suggestion sound more casual or friendly.  
• Extra examples:  
  - "Eet zelf maar." (Just eat yourself.)  
  - "Neem zelf maar een stoel." (Just take a chair yourself.)  
  - "Kies zelf maar." (Just choose yourself.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Lees het boek zelf maar." (Just read the book yourself.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of "maar" softens commands in Dutch, making them more polite and less direct. It's a common way to make requests sound friendlier.

sentences.nl: De flesjes staan in de koelkast, op het tweede plankje.
sentences.en: The bottles are in the fridge, on the second shelf.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The bottles stand in the refrigerator, on the second shelf.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "De flesjes" is the plural diminutive form of "de fles" (the bottle), indicating small bottles.  
• "Staan" is used here because bottles are upright. Dutch uses "staan," "liggen," or "zitten" depending on the position.  
• Word order follows the typical Dutch structure: Subject + Verb + Rest.  
• "Op het tweede plankje" uses the preposition "op" (on) indicating location.

Examples:  
- De boeken liggen op de tafel. (The books lie on the table.)  
- De kinderen zitten in de klas. (The children sit in the class.)  
- De kat ligt op de bank. (The cat lies on the couch.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De glazen staan in de kast, naast de borden. (The glasses stand in the cupboard, next to the plates.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• In Dutch households, it is common to organize items in the fridge or cupboards in a specific order, often with designated shelves for certain items to maximize space and access.

sentences.nl: Dankjewel.
sentences.en: Thank you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Thank you.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dankjewel" is an informal way to say "thank you" in Dutch. It combines "dank" (thank) with "je" (you) and "wel" (well).  
• "Dankjewel" is often used among friends or in casual settings.  
• Extensions:  
  - "Dank u wel." (Thank you. - formal)  
  - "Bedankt voor je hulp." (Thanks for your help.)  
  - "Heel erg bedankt." (Thank you very much.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dankjewel voor het cadeau." (Thank you for the gift.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, expressing gratitude is common in both formal and informal settings. "Dankjewel" is used in casual conversations, while "Dank u wel" is reserved for more formal interactions or when showing respect to someone older or in a position of authority.

sentences.nl: Wil jij ook iets? — Eh… voor mij een wijntje.
sentences.en: Do you want something too? — Uh… a little wine for me.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wil jij ook iets? — Eh… voor mij een wijntje.  
  (Want you also something? — Uh… for me a little wine.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wil jij ook iets?" uses inverted word order for questions, placing "wil" before "jij."  
• "Voor mij" (for me) indicates preference or choice.  
• "Wijntje" is a diminutive form, often used to convey familiarity or casualness.

Examples:  
• Heb jij ook een pen? (Do you also have a pen?)  
• Voor hem een koffie. (For him, a coffee.)  
• Wil je een broodje? (Do you want a sandwich?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wil je nog iets anders? — Eh… voor mij een theetje. (Do you want anything else? — Uh… for me, a little tea.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, diminutives like "wijntje" are often used to make requests sound more casual and friendly.

sentences.nl: Waar staat de wijn? — Er staat een flesje, in het derde kastje van rechts.
sentences.en: Where is the wine? — There is a bottle in the third cabinet from the right.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Where stands the wine? — There stands a bottle, in the third cabinet from right.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Waar staat de wijn?" uses "waar" (where) to ask about location, and "staat" (stands) indicates the position of the wine.  
• "Er staat een flesje" uses "er" as an anticipatory subject combined with "staat" (stands) to indicate the presence of something.  
• "In het derde kastje van rechts" uses ordinal numbers ("derde" - third) and direction ("van rechts" - from right) to specify location.  

Extra Examples:  
• Waar ligt de sleutel? (Where is the key?)  
• Er ligt een boek op de tafel. (There is a book on the table.)  
• In de tweede lade van links vind je de vorken. (In the second drawer from the left, you will find the forks.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Waar staat de lamp? — Er staat een lamp, naast de bank. (Where is the lamp? — There is a lamp, next to the couch.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Cabinets ("kastjes") are commonly used in Dutch homes for storage in kitchens and living areas. They are often labeled by their position (e.g., "van rechts" or "van links") to indicate an exact location.

sentences.nl: Nou, proost!
sentences.en: Well, cheers!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Well, cheers!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Nou" is an interjection often used to express a variety of emotions including surprise, encouragement, or transition. In this context, it sets the tone for a toast.  
• "Proost" is an exclamation used when toasting with drinks, similar to "cheers" in English.

• Examples:  
  - "Nou, laten we beginnen." (Well, let's start.)  
  - "Proost op een goede gezondheid!" (Cheers to good health!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Nou, laten we gaan!" (Well, let's go!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, saying "proost" is a common practice when clinking glasses before drinking. It's considered polite and part of social etiquette in gatherings.

sentences.nl: Proost!
sentences.en: Cheers!

sentences.nl: Eerst koken we de aardappeltjes.
sentences.en: First, we cook the potatoes.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• First cook we the potatoes.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Eerst" means "first" and is used to indicate the sequence of actions.  
• The sentence uses inverted word order because it starts with a time element ("Eerst"), which is common in Dutch to emphasize the order of actions.  
• "Koken" is the verb "to cook" in the present tense.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Eerst ontbijten we, dan gaan we naar school." (First we have breakfast, then we go to school.)  
  - "Eerst lees ik het boek, daarna schrijf ik de samenvatting." (First I read the book, then I write the summary.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Eerst maken we het huiswerk. (First we do the homework.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Potatoes are a staple in Dutch cuisine and are commonly prepared in various ways, such as boiling, frying, or mashing.

sentences.nl: Schil jij de aardappeltjes? — Dat is goed.
sentences.en: Do you peel the potatoes? — That's fine.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Peel you the little potatoes? — That is good.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the present tense "schil" for the verb "schillen" (to peel). In questions, the subject "jij" follows the verb.  
• "Aardappeltjes" is the diminutive form of "aardappelen" (potatoes), often used to convey small size or affection.  
• The phrase "dat is goed" is a common expression meaning "that's good" or "that's fine."  
• Example 1: "Maak jij de salade?" (Are you making the salad?)  
• Example 2: "Dat is leuk." (That is nice.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kook jij de aardappeltjes? (Are you cooking the little potatoes?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Potatoes are a staple in Dutch cuisine and are often served boiled, mashed, or fried.

sentences.nl: Heb je een mesje? — Ja, hier is een aardappelmesje.
sentences.en: Do you have a knife? — Yes, here is a paring knife.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Have you a little knife? — Yes, here is a potato knife.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Heb je" is a common structure for asking if someone has something, similar to "Do you have" in English.  
• "Een mesje" uses the diminutive form of "mes" (knife), indicating a smaller or friendlier version of a knife. The "-je" suffix is a common way to form diminutives in Dutch.  
• "Hier is" means "here is" or "here's," which is a straightforward way to present or hand something over.

Examples:  
• Heb je een pen? (Do you have a pen?)  
• Hier is je boek. (Here is your book.)  
• Heb je een vraag? (Do you have a question?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Heb je een vorkje? — Ja, hier is een dessertvorkje. (Do you have a little fork? — Yes, here is a dessert fork.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives like "mesje" and "aardappelmesje" in Dutch can convey endearment or indicate a smaller size, and they are very common in everyday conversation.

sentences.nl: Dan snijd ik ondertussen de courgette in plakjes, en doe die in de oven.
sentences.en: In the meantime, I slice the zucchini and put it in the oven.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then cut I meanwhile the zucchini into slices, and do those in the oven.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence begins with "Dan" (Then), indicating a sequence of actions.  
• "Snijd" is the first person singular form of "snijden," meaning "to cut." The subject "ik" (I) follows the verb due to the inversion caused by the adverb "Dan."  
• "Ondertussen" means "meanwhile," showing simultaneous action.  
• The definite article "de" is used with "courgette" (zucchini), referring to a specific zucchini.  
• "In plakjes" means "into slices," using the preposition "in" to describe the transformation.  
• "Doe" is the first person singular form of "doen," meaning "to do" or "to put," and "die" (those) refers to "plakjes" (slices).  

Extra Phrases:  
• "Dan ga ik naar de winkel." (Then I go to the store.)  
• "Ondertussen kijk ik naar de film." (Meanwhile, I watch the movie.)  
• "Ik snijd de appel in stukjes." (I cut the apple into pieces.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dan bak ik ondertussen de aardappelen in de pan." (Then I fry the potatoes in the pan.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No related culture notes.

sentences.nl: De aardappeltjes zijn klaar.
sentences.en: The potatoes are ready.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The little potatoes are ready.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Aardappeltjes" is the diminutive form of "aardappelen" (potatoes), often used to express endearment or to make it sound less formal.  
• "Zijn klaar" uses the verb "zijn" (to be) in the present tense, combined with "klaar" (ready) to indicate completion or readiness.  
• Example 1: "De koekjes zijn klaar." (The cookies are ready.)  
• Example 2: "De soep is klaar." (The soup is ready.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "De taart is klaar." (The cake is ready.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch cuisine, potatoes are a staple and are often served in various forms, such as mashed, boiled, or fried. Diminutives like "aardappeltjes" can convey a sense of familiarity or affection for the dish.

sentences.nl: Waar vind ik een pannetje? — Hier, in het tweede kastje.
sentences.en: Where can I find a pan? — Here, in the second cupboard.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Where find I a little pan? — Here, in the second cabinet.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence uses the inverted word order typical in Dutch questions, where the verb "vind" (find) comes before the subject "ik" (I).  
• "Pannetje" is a diminutive form, indicated by the suffix "-tje," meaning "little pan." Diminutives are common in Dutch.  
• "In het tweede kastje" uses a definite article "het" and ordinal number "tweede" (second) to specify location.

• Extra sentences:  
  - "Waar eet jij vanavond?" (Where are you eating tonight?)  
  - "In het derde boek staat het antwoord." (The answer is in the third book.)  
  - "Ik zoek een stoeltje." (I am looking for a little chair.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Waar kan ik een lepeltje vinden?" (Where can I find a little spoon?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Marieke doet water in de pan.
sentences.en: Marieke puts water in the pan.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke does water in the pan.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Doet" is the third-person singular form of "doen," which means "to do" or "to put" in this context.  
• The structure "doet [object] in [location]" is used to describe putting something into a specified place.  
• "In de pan" uses the preposition "in" to indicate the location where the action occurs.

Examples:  
• Jan doet melk in de koffie. (Jan puts milk in the coffee.)  
• Zij doet de boeken in de tas. (She puts the books in the bag.)  
• Hij doet suiker in de thee. (He puts sugar in the tea.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa doet de appels in de schaal. (Lisa puts the apples in the bowl.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No related culture notes.

sentences.nl: Ze zet de aardappeltjes op het vuur.
sentences.en: She puts the potatoes on the fire.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She puts the potatoes on the fire.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zet" is the third person singular present tense of "zetten," meaning "to put" or "to set."  
• "De aardappeltjes" is the diminutive form of "aardappelen," meaning "potatoes." The diminutive often adds a sense of familiarity or affection.  
• "Op het vuur" means "on the fire," where "op" is a preposition indicating placement or position.

• Example 1: "Hij zet de boeken op de plank." (He puts the books on the shelf.)  
• Example 2: "Zij zet de bloemen in de vaas." (She puts the flowers in the vase.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij zet de koffie op tafel. (She puts the coffee on the table.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch cuisine, cooking with "het vuur" often refers to traditional methods like stovetop cooking, which is still common in Dutch households. Diminutives like "aardappeltjes" are frequently used in informal settings to convey warmth or endearment.

sentences.nl: Als laatste bak ik de stukjes vlees.
sentences.en: Finally, I fry the pieces of meat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• As last fry I the pieces meat.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Als laatste" means "as last" and indicates the final step in a sequence.  
• The verb "bakken" (to fry) is in the present tense and follows the subject "ik" (I), which is typical Dutch word order.  
• "De stukjes vlees" means "the pieces of meat," where "stukjes" is a diminutive plural form meaning "small pieces."

• Extra examples:  
  - "Als eerste maak ik de saus." (As first, I make the sauce.)  
  - "Hij bakt de aardappelen in de pan." (He fries the potatoes in the pan.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Als laatste voeg ik de kruiden toe." (As the last step, I add the herbs.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch cooking, meal preparation often emphasizes the order of tasks, as seen with phrases like "als laatste," to ensure optimal timing and flavor development.

sentences.nl: Maar eerst moeten de aardappeltjes gaar zijn.
sentences.en: But first the potatoes need to be cooked.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But first must the potatoes cooked be.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a subordinate clause structure with "maar eerst" (but first) indicating a sequence.  
• "Moeten" is the modal verb meaning "must," and it affects the main verb "zijn" (to be) at the end of the sentence, which is common in Dutch sub-clauses.  
• "Gaar" means "cooked" or "done," often used for food readiness.

Examples:  
• "Eerst moeten we boodschappen doen." (First we must do groceries.)  
• "Maar eerst moet je je huiswerk maken." (But first, you must do your homework.)  
• "De groenten moeten gaar zijn voor het serveren." (The vegetables must be cooked before serving.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maar eerst moeten we de tafel dekken." (But first, we must set the table.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Potatoes are a staple in Dutch cuisine, often served boiled, mashed, or fried. The readiness of potatoes is a common topic in Dutch cooking.

sentences.nl: We moeten dus even wachten.
sentences.en: So we have to wait a while.

sentences.nl: Wat gaan we doen na het eten? — Eh… wat vind je leuk? — Ik wil graag naar een typisch Amsterdams kroegje.
sentences.en: What shall we do after dinner? — Uh... what do you like? — I would like to go to a typical Amsterdam pub.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat gaan we doen na het eten? — Eh… wat vind je leuk? — Ik wil graag naar een typisch Amsterdams kroegje.  
• What go we do after the meal? — Eh… what find you nice? — I want gladly to a typical Amsterdam pub.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Gaan" (go) is used here as an auxiliary verb to indicate a future action.  
• "Na het eten" (after the meal) uses "na" (after) as a preposition to indicate time.  
• "Wat vind je leuk?" (what find you nice?) uses "vinden" (find) to express liking something. This structure is common in Dutch to ask about preferences.  
• "Ik wil graag" (I want gladly) is a polite way to express a wish or desire. "Graag" softens the request.  
  
Examples:  
• Wat gaan we morgen doen? (What are we going to do tomorrow?)  
• Vind je het boek leuk? (Do you like the book?)

sentences.nl: Een eindje verderop is een café.
sentences.en: A little further on is a café.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A little further on is a café.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een eindje verderop" translates to "a little further on." "Eindje" is a diminutive of "eind," meaning "end" or "distance," and "verderop" can be translated as "further on" or "a bit further."  
• The sentence uses an inverted word order because it starts with a prepositional phrase ("Een eindje verderop"), which is common in Dutch when emphasizing location.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Een stukje verderop is een park." (A little further on is a park.)  
  - "Even verderop ligt een rivier." (A bit further on lies a river.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een eindje verderop staat een oude molen." (A little further on stands an old mill.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Café" in Dutch can refer to a place that serves both drinks and light meals, and it is often a social hub in Dutch towns and cities, unlike the English "café," which might imply coffee and snacks only.

sentences.nl: Oh wacht…
sentences.en: Oh wait...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh wacht…  
  (Oh wait…)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wacht" is the imperative form of "wachten," which means "to wait." In Dutch, the imperative is formed by using the stem of the verb, which is often the same as the infinitive minus "-en."  
• The use of "oh" as an interjection is similar to English and is used to express realization or a sudden thought.

• Additional Examples:  
  - "Wacht even." (Wait a moment.)  
  - "Oh nee, ik vergat mijn sleutels." (Oh no, I forgot my keys.)  
  - "Wacht tot ik klaar ben." (Wait until I am ready.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Oh, ik heb het gevonden." (Oh, I found it.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Interjections like "oh" are commonly used in everyday conversation in Dutch, just as in English, to express emotions such as surprise, realization, or frustration.

sentences.nl: En die komt hier om 9 uur voetbal kijken.
sentences.en: And he's coming here to watch football at 9 o'clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And that one comes here at 9 o'clock football watch.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a simple future tense indicated by "komt" (comes), which implies a planned action.  
• The phrase "om 9 uur" indicates time, meaning "at 9 o'clock." The preposition "om" is used to specify exact times.  
• "Voetbal kijken" is a common verb-noun structure in Dutch for activities, meaning "to watch football."

Extra phrases:  
• "Hij komt om 8 uur eten." (He comes at 8 o'clock to eat.)  
• "Zij gaat om 7 uur hardlopen." (She goes running at 7 o'clock.)  
• "Ik ga om 10 uur slapen." (I go to sleep at 10 o'clock.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Watching football is a very popular activity in the Netherlands, especially when national teams or major clubs are playing. Gatherings to watch matches at home are common.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "De achtste finale" translates to "the eighth final," referring to the round of 16 in a tournament. In Dutch, ordinal numbers like "achtste" are used to describe stages in competitions.  
• "Van de" is a common way to express possession or association, similar to "of the" in English.  
• "Champions League" is a proper noun and remains unchanged in Dutch.

• Example phrases:  
  - "De eerste ronde van het toernooi." (The first round of the tournament.)  
  - "De halve finale van de beker." (The semi-final of the cup.)
